results.content: The overall decision model including dimensions, objectives and criteria is tested in the framework of local sensitivity analysis. To clarify our methodological proposal, we also present an illustrative example, based on a real-world application, where we summarise the whole approach and put emphasis on the role of sensitivity analysis as a tool for better understanding the overall decision model and explore its informative content. Consistently with this objective, local sensitivity analysis looks at the sensitivity of rankings obtained with respect to (a) the exclusion/inclusion of different criteria and dimensions; and (b) dimensions and criterion weights changes; all parameters are changed one per time. As one can see in Table 2, describing local sensitivity analysis of dimension weights, options 3 and 6 confirm their winning performance, in fact in the 67.33% of cases 6 occupies the first position while 3 in the 32.67%. By analysing Table 3, presenting local sensitivity analysis of criterion weights, one can realise that although option 6 is the winning option in the 67.80% of cases, there are also weighting vectors where options 2 (7.51%), 3 (10.38%) and 4 (14.31%) are also in the first ranking position. 2. results.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Survey Weights | Erin Hartman
results.content: # Sensitivity Analysis for Survey Weights. Survey weighting allows researchers to account for bias in survey samples, due to unit nonresponse or convenience sampling, using measured demographic covariates. Unfortunately, in practice, it is impossible to know whether the estimated survey weights are sufficient to alleviate concerns about bias due to unobserved confounders or incorrect functional forms used in weighting. In the following paper, we propose two sensitivity analyses for the exclusion of important covariates–(1) a sensitivity analysis for partially observed confounders (i.e., variables measured across the survey sample, but not the target population), and (2) a sensitivity analysis for fully unobserved confounders (i.e., variables not measured in either the survey or the target population). * Multilevel calibration weighting for survey data. * Target Estimation and Adjustment Weighting for Survey Nonresponse and Sampling Bias. * A kernel balancing approach for reducing specification assumptions in survey weighting. * Target Selection as Variable Selection: Using the Lasso to Select Auxiliary Vectors for the Construction of Survey Weights.

results.title: Robustness and sensitivity of weighting and aggregation in constructing composite indices - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: Robustness and sensitivity of weighting and aggregation in constructing composite indices - ScienceDirect
# Robustness and sensitivity of weighting and aggregation in constructing composite indices. In general there are five key steps that should be considered when constructing a composite index, one of which is how the indicators should be weighted and aggregated to form the index. This step is critical in index construction, yet there seems to be no documented evidence about making objective weighting and aggregation choices in constructing indices so that they are robust. This sort of evidence would be particularly helpful for deciding whether any of the existing indices for assessing stream health would suffice for assessing the health of a given set of stream data or whether developing a new index is warranted. Thus we designed a simulation study to test the robustness and sensitivity of the weighting and aggregation choices in four existing stream health indices. ► Weighting and aggregating indicators is a critical step in index construction. Fig. 1 illustrates the five key steps to building a composite index, namely (1) defining a theoretical framework to support the index composition; (2) selecting, cleaning and manipulating the raw indicator data; (3) standardizing the data; (4) weighting and aggregating the indicators; and (5) assessing robustness and sensitivity of the index. All decisions made up until this point in constructing indices, especially the key steps of imputing missing values (as part of data preparation), standardization and weighting and aggregation, should be subject to sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the composite index to the particular choices made. This step is critical in index construction, yet there seems to be no documented evidence about making objective weighting and aggregation choices in constructing indices so that they are robust. Thus we designed a simulation study to test the robustness and sensitivity of the weighting and aggregation choices in four existing indices for assessing stream health. Each index is appraised according to whether they address each of the five key construction steps and details of a simulation study for empirically comparing the performance of their weighting and aggregation step is described. The standard step of development of a WQI are – parameter selection, assignment of weights, development of sub-index functions and final aggregation of weighted sub- index values.

results.title: Olympic rankings based on objective weighting schemes - PMC
results.content: In this paper, we propose an objective principal components weighting scheme for all-time Winter Olympic gold, silver and bronze medals based solely on the number of medals won. Furthermore, our implementation of principal components variable reduction strategy results in the identification of silver as the best representative medal count for parsimonious Winter Olympics rankings. To this end, we employ principal components approach to develop objective weighting schemes for gold, silver and bronze medals won at all-time Winter Olympics. Our results, based on the principal component approach to Olympic rankings, suggest that approximately equal weights be assigned to the three types of all-time Winter Olympics medals. Even though we have developed objective weighting schemes for gold, silver and bronze medals won at all-time Winter Olympics, we acknowledge that the principal components approach to Olympic rankings proposed in this paper, like every other ranking methods proposed to date, is not a perfect way to compare countries’ performances.
